entries.title: The 1990s in Japan: A Lost Decade
entries.method: Neoclassical growth model (Hansen-style, indivisible labor, exogenous workweek). It is calibrated to the 1984-88 steady-state period. Exogenous paths for TFP, workweek length and government share are then fed in to see whether the model reproduces the 1990s. Growth accounting and a flow-of-funds check on the credit-crunch hypothesis are also used.
entries.target: Japan, whole economy (aggregate national accounts; nonfinancial corporate sector for the credit-crunch evidence)
entries.period: 1970-1999 for relative per capita GDP; 1984-1999 for the main growth accounting and the model
entries.quantity: Per capita GDP growth, Japan vs US, 1990s
entries.quote: Per capita GDP increased at only 0.6 percent in the 1990s. The comparable figure for the United States was 2.6 percent.
entries.limitation: The model takes the TFP slowdown as exogenous and does not explain its cause (the subsidy hypothesis has only weak support), the text read is the 2000 conference draft rather than the published RED version, and the Japan-US comparison is not a causal identification.

entries.title: Two Decades of Japanese Monetary Policy and the Deflation Problem
entries.method: A narrative and institutional review of Bank of Japan policy, with a policy proposal (price-level targeting and non-conventional measures). It also runs one empirical exercise: Taylor rule regressions of the call rate on the inflation rate and an ad hoc GDP gap, in backward-looking and forward-looking versions. The regressions use heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors, and the GDP gap comes from an adjusted moving-average potential output.
entries.target: Japan (macro and monetary policy; no industry-level analysis)
entries.period: About 1982 to 2004. The Taylor rule regressions use 1982:I to 1994:IV. The narrative covers 1980s to early 2004.
entries.quantity: Average real GDP growth, 1993 to 2003
entries.quote: The average growth rate from 1993 to 2003 is just above 1 percent.
entries.limitation: The Taylor rule estimates cover only 1982-1994, and the authors themselves say they doubt this kind of evidence. The GDP gap is ad hoc and the Durbin-Watson statistics are low (0.162 to 0.662, indicating serial correlation), so identification is weak and the paper gives no cross-country or industry-level estimates.

entries.authors: Caballero, R. J.; Hoshi, T.; Kashyap, A. K.
entries.title: Zombie Lending and Depressed Restructuring in Japan
entries.method: Firm-level classification of zombie firms by whether they received subsidized bank credit (a crisp measure and fuzzy alternatives). The authors then run panel regressions of non-zombie investment, employment growth and a productivity gap on the industry zombie share, with industry and year dummies or industry-by-year dummies. They add counterfactual simulations of cumulative losses and a theoretical model.
entries.target: Japan; publicly traded manufacturing, construction, real estate, retail, wholesale and service firms (about 2360 firms)
entries.period: Firm data 1981-2002; zombie-era comparison of the 1981-1993 average with 1996-2002
entries.quantity: Zombie share of firms in the early 2000s (raw)
entries.quote: roughly 30% of these firms were on life support from the banks in the early 2000s
entries.limitation: The sample covers only listed firms in 1981-2002 and identifies zombies from interest-rate comparisons, so classification is indirect. The industry-share regressions leave room for omitted demand shocks, and the Table 4 figures are partial-equilibrium extrapolations that ignore general-equilibrium feedback.

entries.title: Unnatural Selection: Perverse Incentives and the Misallocation of Credit in Japan
entries.method: 貸し手と企業を結びつけた貸出パネルで、銀行が企業への貸出を増やした確率をlogitで推定する。説明変数は企業の健全性(ROA、流動資産比率、売上成長)、銀行の自己資本比率が規制水準に近いかのダミー(REQ1、REQ2)、主力銀行・同一系列の提携ダミー。標準誤差は年内の誤差相関を許したロバスト標準誤差。別途、貸出増加後の株価変化をOLSで推定。データはPACAP、Bankscope、Nikkei Needs。
entries.target: 日本。東証1部・2部上場企業(3月決算)と市場取引される銀行、非銀行金融機関、政府系銀行の貸出。業種は9産業ダミーで制御し、特定産業の分析ではない。
entries.period: 1993〜1999年(年次データ)。Table 2の株価回帰は1994-98年と1996-98年。
entries.quantity: 総貸出の増加と翌年の株価変化(1996-98年)
entries.unit: 株価変化率(%)に対する係数
entries.locator: Table 2, 第2列; 本文 I節
entries.quote: an increase in total loans to a firm is associated with a decline in the firm’s stock price of about 2.4 percent during the subsequent year
entries.limitation: 作業論文版を読んだ結果であり、「資金配分の悪化が低成長を招いた」という結論は貸出確率のlogit推定と株価回帰に基づく相関的証拠にとどまる(因果の識別は弱い)。対象は上場企業の1993〜1999年のみで、IT・参入・規制への直接の推定値はなく、他国への一般化もできない。

entries.authors: Kwon, H. U.; Narita, F.; Narita, M.
entries.title: Resource reallocation and zombie lending in Japan in the 1990s
entries.method: Petrin-Levinsohn decomposition of aggregate productivity growth (APG) into technical efficiency, reallocation and net entry using plant-level data. A Restuccia-Rogerson-type heterogeneous-plant model is calibrated, and a no-zombie-lending counterfactual is run. Zombies are plants whose technical efficiency stays below the 20th percentile for five consecutive years.
entries.target: Japan, manufacturing plants (plant-level data)
entries.quantity: Average reallocation term, 1980s
entries.quote: The average reallocation term was -0.18% during the 1980s and it was -0.85% during the 1990s.
entries.limitation: The read text is the RIETI Discussion Paper 09-E-052 (2009), not the 2015 RED journal text, which was behind a redirect, so the published numbers may differ; the study covers manufacturing only, and the zombie share comes from a calibrated model rather than a causal identification.

entries.title: Information Technology and the Japanese Economy
entries.method: Growth accounting on the production possibility frontier (Jorgenson 1995c/2002b). Japanese SNA93 data adjusted to U.S. NIPA definitions, with added prepackaged and own-account software investment, new constant-quality IT price deflators, and capital services imputed for households and government. TFP is split into IT and Non-IT by the dual (price) approach. Scenario projections for 2003-2013. There are no standard errors or confidence intervals; it is a deterministic accounting decomposition.
entries.target: Japan vs United States, aggregate economy (GDP, IT-producing vs Non-IT sectors); NBER WP 11801
entries.quantity: Japan TFP growth, 1995-03 (Table 4)
entries.quote: Total Factor Productivity 1.57 1.25 0.80 0.45
entries.limitation: This is descriptive growth accounting with no standard errors or causal identification; it rests on the authors' constructed IT price deflators and imputations (the Japanese capital stock data of the 1970s are noted as less reliable), the data end in 2003, the projections are scenario-based, and the paper does not directly measure entry, regulation or catch-up mechanisms.

entries.title: Intangible Investment in Japan: Measurement and Contribution to Economic Growth
entries.method: Corrado-Hulten-Sichel (2005, 2006) framework applied to the JIP 2008 Database. The authors measure intangible investment (computerized information, innovative property, economic competencies), build an intangible capital stock, and run growth accounting with and without intangible capital. entries.title: Raising the Speed Limit: U.S. Economic Growth in the Information Age
entries.method: Neoclassical growth accounting on a production possibilities frontier (Jorgenson-Griliches), with computers, software and communications equipment as separate outputs and capital inputs. Capital and labor are quality-adjusted and weighted by rental prices and shares. TFP is a residual. Industry-level productivity is aggregated with Domar weights. Data come from the 1999 NIPA benchmark revision, BLS and Census. Three alternative IT price deflation cases are used, and the results are compared with CBO, CEA and OMB growth projections.
entries.target: United States, aggregate private domestic economy plus 1958-96 industry-level analysis (IT-producing vs IT-using industries such as FIRE and other services)

entries.limitation: This is descriptive growth accounting with no causal identification. It covers only the US, mostly through 1998 (1999 figures are preliminary). The IT deflators for software and communications are uncertain, so the IT share of TFP varies from 0.44 to 0.86 percentage points across cases. The paper contains no Japan estimates.

entries.title: The 1990s in Japan: A Lost Decade
entries.method: The authors calibrate a neoclassical growth model with indivisible labor (Hansen 1985), an exogenous workweek, a capital income tax and government purchases to 1984-89 Japanese averages. They feed in the observed paths of TFP, the workweek and the government share of output as exogenous, and compare the predicted 1990s path with the data. The paper also tests the credit-crunch hypothesis, using the flow-of-funds identity for non-financial corporations (SNA and MOF Hojin Kigyo Tokei Kiho survey data) and Bernanke-Lown-style cross-section regressions of GDP and employment growth on bank loan growth in recessions.
entries.target: Japan, whole economy (aggregate, not by industry), with a US and Western Europe comparison. Also non-financial corporations (large and small firms) for the credit-crunch tests, and prefectures and cities for the loan-growth regressions.
entries.period: Calibration on 1984-88/89 averages. Model simulation and data from 1990 to 1999 (data to FY1998 for flow of funds). Per capita GDP comparison 1970-1999. Cross-section recession windows 1979-82, 1990-93 and 1996-98.
entries.quantity: Japan TFP growth rate, 1984-91 average
entries.locator: Sec. 3.1, 'TFP growth falls subsequent to 1991', p.10
entries.quote: TFP growth in the 1984-91 period averaged 2.0 percent per year.
entries.limitation: The text read is the October 2000 preliminary conference draft rather than the published 2002 RED version. TFP is treated as an exogenous residual whose fall is unexplained, so this is calibration and not causal identification. It rests on one country, mostly on aggregate data, and the credit-crunch rejection relies on indirect evidence. Several figures and a few characters were garbled in the PDF text extraction, and the figure contents could not be read.

entries.title: Americans Do IT Better: US Multinationals and the Productivity Miracle
entries.method: Establishment-level production function (log gross output on materials, labour, non-IT capital, IT capital) with IT elasticity allowed to differ by ownership (US MNE, non-US MNE, domestic). OLS and establishment fixed effects, GMM system and Olley-Pakes checks, and a pre/post takeover sample (establishments taken over by US vs non-US multinationals). A model with organization-IT complementarity and labour-market-regulation adjustment costs is also presented.
entries.target: UK establishments (ABI panel, manufacturing and services incl. retail, wholesale), comparing US multinationals, non-US multinationals and domestic firms; macro motivation US vs Europe
entries.period: 1995-2003 (UK establishment panel)
entries.quantity: US labour productivity growth in IT-using sectors, 1990-95 vs 1995-2001 (O'Mahony and Van Ark, cited)
entries.value_raw: 1.2% per annum to 4.7% per annum (US); 2% pre and post 1995 (Europe)
entries.quote: US productivity growth in sectors that intensively used IT accelerated by 3.5 percentage points between 1995 and 2001 (from 1.2% per annum to 4.7% per annum).
entries.limitation: Numbers come from the 2007 NBER working paper, not the paywalled AER text, so published values may differ; the results are UK-only OLS/fixed-effects correlations with limited identification (takeover design, no instrument), a 1995-2003 sample, and do not cover Japan.

entries.title: Does the "New Economy" Measure up to the Great Inventions of the Past?
entries.method: Growth accounting that decomposes the U.S. productivity revival into cyclical and trend parts and into durable manufacturing versus the rest of the economy, with multifactor productivity (MFP) subtracting the contribution of computer investment. A historical comparison with the five clusters of 1860-1900 inventions. Analysis of computer price and quantity data to test whether the Internet raised demand for computers.
entries.target: United States, private economy: durable manufacturing (computers, peripherals, telecommunications equipment) versus the rest. The paper compares the "New Economy" with the Great Inventions of 1860-1900. It contains no Japan estimates.
entries.period: 1995-99 compared with 1972-95; the "golden age" of 1913-72; Great Inventions of 1860-1900
entries.quantity: Cyclical component of the revival
entries.quote: 0.54 of an unsustainable cyclical effect
entries.limitation: This is the working-paper version and only the abstract and introduction were read; the decomposition tables and the JEP edition were not checked. The estimates are U.S. growth-accounting results for the short 1995-99 window, and the cyclical/trend split is not a causal identification, so the finding should not be carried over to Japan directly.

entries.title: Structural Transformation in Africa: Static Gains, Dynamic Losses
entries.method: Shift-share decomposition of labour productivity growth into a within effect and a between (reallocation) effect. The between effect is split into a static part (reallocation to sectors with above-average productivity levels) and a dynamic part (reallocation to sectors with above-average productivity growth). It uses the new Africa Sector Database (10 sectors, value added and persons engaged) and sector-specific PPPs for international productivity levels. Results are compared with Asia and Latin America using the GGDC 10-sector database. Country results are unweighted averages.
entries.target: 11 Sub-Saharan African countries (Botswana, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Mauritius, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia), with the whole economy split into 10 ISIC rev. 3 sectors. Latin America and Asia are used for comparison.
entries.period: 1960-2010. Sub-periods are 1960-1975, 1975-1990 and 1990-2010. The start year varies by country.
entries.quantity: Decomposition of annual labour productivity growth, equation (4), 1960-2010, unweighted average of 11 countries: total, within, static between, dynamic between
entries.quote: The dynamic contribution of -0.8 per cent suggests that the marginal productivity of additional workers in expanding sectors has been below that of existing activities.
entries.limitation: The results are descriptive shift-share accounting with no causal identification, and the data are unweighted averages across 11 sub-Saharan countries with weak national accounts, employment and informal-sector coverage. The numbers come from the 2013 working paper rather than the 2015 journal text, and the paper has no Japan content, so the transfer to Japan is only an analogy.

entries.title: Zombie Lending and Depressed Restructuring in Japan
entries.method: Zombie firms are identified by comparing each firm's actual interest payments with a hypothetical minimum (risk-free) interest bill. Firms paying below the minimum are crisp zombies, and fuzzy variants are also used. The authors build a model of zombie congestion, then run firm-level panel regressions on non-zombies' investment (I/K), employment growth and productivity. The regressors are the industry zombie share (asset-weighted) and its interaction with a non-zombie dummy. Specifications use industry and year dummies, or industry-by-year dummies. Counterfactual losses in Table 4 are extrapolated from the coefficients.
entries.target: Japan. Publicly traded manufacturing, construction, real estate, retail, wholesale (excluding nine general trading companies) and service firms, 1,844 to 2,506 firms depending on the year.
entries.period: 1981-2002, with the zombie wave in the 1990s; counterfactual losses are computed for 1993-2002.
entries.quantity: Share of listed firms that were zombies, raw count, early 2000s
entries.quote: The top panel of the figure shows roughly 30% of these firms were on life support from the banks in the early 2000s.
entries.limitation: Identification rests on cross-industry variation in a constructed interest-payment-based zombie measure, so reverse causality and omitted industry shocks are not fully excluded, and the sample covers only listed Japanese firms in 1981-2002.

entries.title: The Industry Origins of Japanese Economic Growth
entries.method: Industry-level growth accounting in the Jorgenson system of national accounts. It capitalizes own-account and pre-packaged software and uses Japan's quality-adjusted "best practice" IT prices. The paper reports aggregate TFP built from industry TFP with Domar weights, and also a measure called aggregate production function TFP (Table 3).
entries.target: Japan, whole economy and 47 industries, including the IT-producing industries (Computers, Communications Equipment, Electronic Components). Compared with the US figures of Jorgenson, Ho and Stiroh (2005).
entries.quantity: Aggregate TFP contribution to value-added growth, 1990-1995
entries.quote: In the early 1990s aggregate TFP turns negative. The overall contribution is –0.48 percent
entries.limitation: This is a descriptive growth-accounting decomposition with no causal identification. TFP is a residual that depends on the price deflators and on the Domar-weight aggregation; the paper's own Table 3 shows aggregate production function TFP exceeding aggregate TFP by over 1.0 percent per year in the 1990s. The US comparison rests on a different period (1977-2000) and a different dataset, and the numbers come from the NBER working-paper version rather than the journal version.

entries.title: Information Technology and the Japanese Economy
entries.method: Growth accounting on a production possibility frontier (Jorgenson 1995c). Japanese IT investment data were adjusted to U.S. NIPA definitions. This included new software investment data and IT price indexes based on BOJ chain-weighted series plus internationally harmonized prices. Output and input contributions are decomposed into IT capital, non-IT capital, labor and TFP. The 2003-2013 base, optimistic and pessimistic projections are scenario assumptions built from past averages.

entries.quote: Gross Domestic Product 4.03 3.97 1.64 1.28
entries.limitation: This is descriptive growth accounting with no causal identification. It depends on constructed IT price deflators and software data, the period ends in 2003, and the projections rest on assumed averages and an assumed labor-force path, so the Japan-US comparison inherits definitional adjustments and says nothing directly about entry, regulation or catch-up mechanisms.

entries.title: The 1990s in Japan: A Lost Decade
entries.method: Neoclassical growth model calibrated to the 1984-88 steady-growth period. TFP, workweek length and the government purchases share are taken as exogenous, and the model is used to predict the 1990s. Supporting growth accounting. The draft also tests the credit-crunch view with SNA flow-of-funds identities, MOF corporate survey data and a cross-section regression of growth on loan growth.
entries.target: Japan, aggregate economy (macro, non-government capital and corporate sector), with comparisons to the US and Western Europe
entries.period: 1984-1999 data; model calibrated to 1984-88/89 and simulated for the 1990s. Per capita GDP shown for 1970-1999.
entries.quantity: Japan TFP growth, 1984-91
entries.locator: Sec. 3.1, 'TFP growth falls subsequent to 1991', p.10
entries.quote: TFP growth in the 1984-91 period averaged 2.0 percent per year.
entries.limitation: These figures come from a preliminary conference draft that the authors asked not to be quoted, so they may differ from the published RED 2002 text. TFP is a growth-accounting residual with no causal identification, the subsidy explanation is only a conjecture supported by one episode (1978-83), and the draft does not test IT, entry or regulation directly.

entries.title: The Role of the Structural Transformation in Aggregate Productivity
entries.method: A simple structural-transformation model calibrated to the US growth experience is used to measure sectoral labor productivity differences across countries. Sectoral productivity series are fed into the model. Counterfactuals then switch off sectoral productivity growth: no industry growth, no services growth, US growth in every sector, or services catch-up to the industry level. Each is compared with the model path for relative aggregate productivity.
entries.target: 29 countries: OECD and Latin American economies, plus Japan, Korea and Turkey. Three sectors: agriculture, industry, services. Japan sample 1960-2004; Korea 1972-2003.
entries.period: Country samples start between 1950 and 1972 and end 2002-2004. The data give value added per hour and shares of hours. Series are HP-filtered with lambda=100.
entries.quantity: Share of cross-country aggregate productivity catch-up explained by industry productivity catch-up
entries.value_raw: about 50 percent (6.8 p.p. of 12.8 in the model)
entries.unit: percent of the change in relative aggregate productivity
entries.locator: Section on counterfactuals (no/US-level industry growth), p.27 of the working paper
entries.quote: productivity catch-up in industry explains about 50 percent (6.8 p.p. of 12.8 in the model) of the relative aggregate productivity gains observed during the sample period.
entries.limitation: The results are model-based counterfactuals calibrated to the US, with no identification of causal drivers. Sector labor productivity is measured from cross-country national accounts data. Japan appears only as one of 29 countries, with no Japan-specific figures beyond the counterfactual exception. All figures are from the working paper version and need checking against the published QJE text.

entries.title: Misallocation and Manufacturing TFP in China and India
entries.method: Monopolistic competition model with heterogeneous plant TFPQ. Plant-level gaps in marginal products (TFPR dispersion) are measured within 4-digit industries. TFP gains are computed by hypothetically reallocating capital and labor to equalize TFPR, either fully or to the U.S. level of dispersion. Elasticity of substitution within industries is sigma=3.
entries.target: Manufacturing plants in China (Chinese industrial firm data) and India (Annual Survey of Industries), with the U.S. as benchmark
entries.quantity: Manufacturing TFP gain from moving to U.S. efficiency, China
entries.quote: we calculate manufacturing TFP gains of 30-50% in China and 40-60% in India.
entries.limitation: Gains rest on structural assumptions (sigma=3, no measurement error, no adjustment costs or markup variation), and the authors say that errors in these could overstate the results, which they show are very sensitive to sigma. The data cover only 1987-2005 for China and India and do not identify policy causes.

entries.title: Policy distortions and aggregate productivity with heterogeneous establishments
entries.method: Growth model with heterogeneous plants, entry and exit, and decreasing returns. It is calibrated to US data (plant size distribution, job destruction rate). Policies are modelled as idiosyncratic output taxes and subsidies, with or without correlation to plant productivity. Steady states are compared with the undistorted benchmark.

entries.title: Cross-Country Differences in Productivity: The Role of Allocation and Selection
entries.method: Harmonized firm-level moments built by "distributed micro-data analysis" of business registers, tax rolls and enterprise surveys. The authors compute the within-industry Olley-Pakes (OP) covariance between employment share and log revenue labor productivity, plus the within-industry standard deviations of labor productivity and TFP. Industry weights are time-invariant US weights. A heterogeneous-firm model is then calibrated with overhead labor, quasi-fixed capital, entry costs and idiosyncratic output distortions. The model is matched to the US survival rate and OP covariance, then the distortion distribution is chosen to match each country's OP covariance exactly.
entries.target: Manufacturing in 8 countries: US, UK, Germany, France, Netherlands, plus the transition economies Hungary, Romania and Slovenia. Japan is not covered. The harmonized database as a whole covers up to 24 countries.
entries.period: Data cover 1992-2001 (France only to 1995). Changes in Table 2 compare the 1996-2001 average with the 1992-1995 average. The text also says 1996-2001 versus 1991-1995, which is inconsistent with the Table 2 note.
entries.quantity: OP covariance term, Western Europe (Table 1)
entries.quote: the OP covariance term only reaches 20-30 log points in Western Europe
entries.limitation: The OP covariance is a descriptive accounting moment and the distortions are inferred from a calibrated model rather than identified causally. The data are manufacturing only, 1992-2001, and use revenue-based labor productivity, and the model matches dispersion in labor productivity and TFP poorly, especially in the transition economies. The IT, regulation and entry-barrier effects the task asked about are not estimated in this text. Only the model's entry cost and survival rate are reported.

entries.title: Regulation, productivity and growth: OECD evidence
entries.method: Industry-level panel regression of multifactor productivity (MFP) growth. The model has a technology-catch-up (conditional convergence) form. Regressors are leader-country MFP growth, the lagged technology gap to the frontier, and human capital. Product market regulation, entry liberalisation, entry barriers and privatisation indicators are added, directly and interacted with the technology gap. The estimator is fixed effects with industry and time dummies, plus country dummies where the indicator varies over time. Standard errors are robust, or clustered by country-industry when country dummies are dropped. 64 outliers were removed, and the sample is 3,101 observations. MFP comes from OECD STAN, with industry-specific expenditure PPPs and Caves et al. multilateral indices.
entries.target: 18 OECD countries, including Japan. 17 manufacturing and 6 business-services industries (23 two-digit industries). Countries: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, France, West Germany, Greece, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, UK and US.
entries.period: 1984-1998 (industry MFP panel). The regulation indicators are mostly 1998 values (economy-wide and industry-level) plus time-series indicators of entry liberalisation and privatisation.
entries.quantity: Overall privatisation, effect on MFP growth (Table 6 eq.1, country dummies included)
entries.quote: The coefficient of the privatisation variable is generally positive and significant at conventional levels, suggesting that countries in which privatisation was more extensive benefited from persistent productivity gains.
entries.limitation: Regulation indicators are largely 1998 cross-sections with no time dimension, so the regressions drop country dummies and identification is weak (the authors flag mis-specification and RESET concerns). Several coefficients are only significant at 10%, the simulations focus on Europe rather than Japan, the period ends in 1998, and the source is the working-paper version rather than the journal text.

entries.title: Why Did Japan's TFP Growth Slow Down in the Lost Decade? An Empirical Analysis Based on Firm-Level Data of Manufacturing Firms
entries.method: Firm-level TFP is computed from METI's Kigyo Katsudo Kihon Chosa (Basic Survey on Business Activities by Enterprises), using gross output. Industry TFP growth is decomposed with the Baily-Hulten-Campbell / Foster-Haltiwanger-Krizan method into within, between, covariance, entry and exit effects (switch-in and switch-out are included in entry and exit). The paper then tracks the TFP gap between the 75th and 25th percentile firms and compares high-TFP and low-TFP firm groups. It also runs pooled regressions of firm TFP growth on R&D intensity, internationalization, size, leverage and other variables, with beta-convergence terms.
entries.target: Japan, manufacturing sector (30 industries), firm-level data
entries.period: 1994-2001 (TFP growth decomposition, and TFP-gap analysis); regression for 1995-2001, split 1995-1997 and 1998-2001
entries.quantity: Manufacturing TFP growth over 1994-2001 and its within-firm effect (Japan)
entries.interval_raw: Shares of total in parentheses: within 0.56
entries.limitation: The text read is the 2004 working-paper version, not the 2006 journal text. The exit measure also counts firms that shrank below the survey cut-off, merged or changed industry, and the US and Korea comparators use establishment data, so the decomposition is descriptive and does not identify causes.

entries.title: Aggregate Productivity Growth: Lessons from Microeconomic Evidence
entries.method: Decomposition of industry productivity growth (multifactor and labor productivity) into within-plant, between-plant, cross, and net-entry terms. Two weighting methods are used: method 1 uses fixed initial weights, and method 2 uses average-share weights. Ten- and five-year horizons are compared. Regressions on plant productivity levels include year, 4-digit industry, and entry/exit dummies. The service-sector analysis links Census of Services establishment data over time with PPN, EIN, and name/address matching (Automatch).
entries.target: US manufacturing establishments (Census of Manufactures / LRD; includes SIC 3312 steel) and the US service industry of automobile repair shops (SIC 753, 4-digit components; Census of Services)
entries.period: Manufacturing: 1977-87 ten-year changes, and five-year changes 1977-82, 1982-87, 1987-92. Services: 1987-92 (Census of Services).
entries.quantity: Contribution of net entry to multifactor productivity growth, ten-year 1977-87 manufacturing; compared with output shares of exiting and entering plants
entries.value_raw: 25 percent (exiting plants' output share 22 percent; entering plants' activity share 21 percent)
entries.locator: Sec. V.C, p. 35 (Table 9 panel A vs Table 4)
entries.quote: the contribution of net entry to multifactor productivity is 25 percent while the share of output accounted for by exiting plants is 22 percent
entries.limitation: The analysis is a US-only accounting decomposition for 1977-92. It is not causal, and the authors say the results are sensitive to the decomposition method and to measurement error. The service evidence covers a single industry (automobile repair shops), which the authors call exploratory. The paper does not examine IT, regulation, or Japan, and I did not read the Sec. III literature review or the tables, so any figures taken from tables are missing.

entries.authors: Cette, Lopez, Mairesse, Nicoletti (NBER版: Bourlès, Cette, Lopez, Mairesse)
entries.title: Do Product Market Regulations in Upstream Sectors Curb Productivity Growth? Panel Data Evidence for OECD Countries
entries.method: Aghion et al. (1997) の新シュンペーター型内生成長モデルを拡張した。上流の競争が弱いと、下流の効率改善で得られるレントを上流が取り込み、下流の改善意欲が下がる。パネル OLS で MFP 成長率を、技術フロンティアの MFP 変化、フロンティアとの距離(gap)、上流規制負担指標(産業連関で下流に波及させた値)、およびその gap との交差項に回帰した。国×時間と産業の固定効果を入れた。規制の効果が gap によって変わることを許している。規制指標は 0-6 のスケールのもので、論文は 0-1 に変換して使っている。
entries.target: OECD 15か国・20産業(非農業の事業部門)。上流の非製造業(エネルギー、運輸、通信、小売、専門サービス、金融など)の参入規制が、産業連関を通じて下流産業の MFP 成長に与える影響。表2の対象国はスウェーデン、オランダ、デンマーク、豪州、米国、フィンランド、ドイツ、カナダ、ベルギー、スペイン、ノルウェー、フランス、イタリア、オーストリア、ギリシャ。日本は含まれない。
entries.quantity: 1985-2007 全期間の上流規制負担の係数(交差項あり、平均で評価)

entries.title: Regulation and Investment
entries.method: Dynamic panel regression of the sector investment rate (I/K) by OLS. It uses two lags of I/K, up to two lags of one of four regulation indices (REGOL overall, REGNO excluding public ownership, BEVI barriers to entry, REGPO public ownership), country and sector fixed effects, and common or sector-specific year dummies. The paper reports the sum of the regulation coefficients and the implied long-run coefficient. Extensions cover fiscal and labor-market controls, value added to capital, heterogeneous short-run responses, and non-linear effects.
entries.target: 21 OECD countries for the regulation indicators. The investment panels cover 8 countries (Panel A) or 12 (Panel B), which include Japan for the utilities sector only in Panel B. Sectors are utilities (electricity and gas), communications (telecoms and post) and transport (airlines, road freight, rail).
entries.period: 1975-1996 for the regulation indicators in the data section (Figure 1 compares 1975 and 1998). Investment data from the OECD STAN and ISDB databases.
entries.quantity: Long-run effect on investment rate of a one-unit decrease in REGOL (Panel A, Model 2, common year effects)
entries.interval_raw: Standard errors not reported. Sum of coefficients -0.0017, p=0.0042
entries.locator: Section 4.1, p.15; Table 1 Panel A Model 2
entries.quote: The investment rate increases by 1.1 percentage points in the long-run. Since the investment rate is approximately equal to 6% on average, this would imply an increase to 7.1%.
entries.limitation: The evidence is a regulation-investment association in 1975-1998 utilities, transport and communications panels, with identification resting on lagged OLS regressors and fixed effects rather than exogenous variation. Japan appears only in utilities, the data end before the 2000s IT era, and the version read is the 2003 working paper, not the JEEA text.

entries.title: Entry and Productivity Growth: Evidence from Microlevel Panel Data
entries.method: A reduced-form panel regression (eq. 5) of establishment-level TFP growth, computed with a superlative index, on the change in the industry share of employment in foreign plants. The data are the ARD (Annual Respondents Database) and are weighted by inverse sampling probability times employment. The OLS models have year effects and either 4-digit industry dummies or establishment fixed effects. The IV/2SLS models instrument entry with indicators for 3-digit industries expected to be strongly or moderately affected by the EU Single Market Program (during 1988-1992 and from 1993 on), plus US R&D intensity at the 2-digit level. The theory is a multisector Schumpeterian model in which entry at the frontier raises innovation by firms close to the frontier and lowers it for firms far below.
entries.target: United Kingdom, domestic incumbent establishments in manufacturing (166 four-digit industries; 3,827 establishments with at least 100 employees in one year and surviving at least four years). The paper measures entry as foreign entry (change in the foreign-plant share of industry employment).
entries.period: 1980 to 1993 (sample 1981-1993 per Table 1 notes)
entries.quantity: Effect of change in foreign plant employment share on incumbent TFP growth, OLS with year and 4-digit industry indicators
entries.unit: coefficient on TFP growth per unit change in foreign employment share
entries.quote: Change(foreign plant employment)jt 0.0857** (0.0397)
entries.limitation: Identification rests on EU Single Market Program industry indicators and US R&D intensity as instruments. The authors themselves note that the results may also reflect selection or spillovers. The study covers only UK manufacturing in 1980-1993, and the measure is foreign-plant employment share, which also picks up expansions, contractions and exits. The IV standard errors are wide, and the first-stage F is moderate in column 3 (4.71).

entries.title: Cross-country evidence on start-up dynamics
entries.method: 各国の事業所統計・企業登記から各国の専門家が共通のStataルーチンを秘匿データ上で実行して作る集計データベース(DynEmp v.2)を使った記述的分析。新規企業の雇用創出への寄与を、開業率、参入時の平均規模、生存率、生存企業の平均成長率の4要素に分解する。分布回帰(OLS、線形確率モデル)の出力も収集するが、本文は主に記述統計と図。因果識別はしない。
entries.target: DynEmp v.2に含まれる16か国(Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Costa Rica, Denmark, Finland, Hungary, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Turkey)の全産業(2桁産業で集計)。日本は含まれない。
entries.period: 大半の国で2002〜2011年。Costa RicaとPortugalは短く、Austria, Brazil, Denmark, Luxembourg, Norway, Swedenは長い。コホート(transition matrices)は2001, 2004, 2007年開始で3, 5, 7年後を追跡。
entries.quantity: 新規参入企業の生存率(参入後3年・5年・7年)
entries.value_raw: just above 60% after three years; about 50% after five years; just over 40% after seven years
entries.quote: the survival rate is on average equal to just above 60% after three years from entry, to about 50% after five years, and to just over 40% after seven years
entries.limitation: 対象は日本を含まない16か国で、中間的なデータセットの記述統計にとどまり、著者自身が国間比較は主目的でないと述べており、因果識別はなく、規制やITの効果推定も本文にはない。

entries.title: Resource reallocation and zombie lending in Japan in the 1990s
entries.method: Aggregate productivity growth (APG) is decomposed into technical efficiency, reallocation and net-entry terms, using a Petrin-Levinsohn-type approach on plant-level production function estimates (proxy estimation). A plant-heterogeneity model is calibrated to those estimates. Zombies are plants with TFP below the 20th percentile for 5 consecutive years, and they face different effective tax wedges (subsidized credit) in the model. A counterfactual with no zombie lending is then compared with the zombie case.
entries.target: Japan, manufacturing plants (plant-level data on manufacturers)
entries.period: 1981-2000 (the 1990s versus the 1980s); the zombie counterfactual compares steady states in 1989 and 1999
entries.quantity: Average reallocation term of APG, 1980s
entries.quote: The average reallocation term was -0.18% during the 1980s and it was -0.85% during the 1990s.
entries.limitation: These numbers come from the 2009 RIETI working paper, not the published RED version. The 37% figure rests on a calibrated model whose zombie definition (below the 20th TFP percentile for 5 years) and tax-wedge identification are assumptions rather than credit data. The sample is manufacturing only, so the result cannot be extended to services.

entries.title: Why was Japan left behind in the ICT revolution?
entries.method: Firm-level data from two METI surveys (Basic Survey of Japanese Business Structure and Activities, and the IT Survey). ICT intensity is compared across four size groups and four age groups. A Cobb-Douglas value-added production function with labor, non-ICT capital and ICT input is estimated by pooled OLS (system GMM was run but not shown). The coefficients vary by size and age group, and year and industry dummies are included. The marginal product of ICT input is then derived by group. Section 5 adds survey evidence and a Japan-US comparison of employment by firm size.
entries.target: Japan, firm-level data covering manufacturing, mining, electricity and gas, commerce and services, with comparisons to the United States and other developed economies

entries.title: The 1990s in Japan: A Lost Decade
entries.method: Neoclassical growth accounting plus a calibrated growth model. It is calibrated to pre-1990 Japanese data, with TFP and the workweek length exogenous. Workweek length is endogenous after 1993. The model then predicts the 1990s path of output, the capital-output ratio and the return on capital. Capital share theta is set to 0.362. The paper also examines financing and investment data for credit-crunch evidence.
entries.target: Japan, aggregate economy (per working-age person aged 20-69, whole economy; no industry breakdown)
entries.period: Mainly 1991-2000 (the 'lost decade'), compared with 1960-1973, 1973-1983 and 1983-1991. The model is calibrated to pre-1990 data and simulated forward to 2001 and beyond.
entries.quantity: Average annual growth of per capita GDP, Japan, 1991-2000
entries.quote: The average annual growth rate of per capita GDP was 0.5 percent in the 1991-2000 period. The comparable figure for the United States was 2.6 percent.
entries.limitation: The paper treats TFP as exogenous and does not explain why it fell. The TFP numbers also differ within the paper (2.4 and 0.2 percent in the text versus 3.7 and 0.3 percent for the TFP factor in Table I), because the two use different definitions. The data are macro aggregates for Japan alone, so the results are model-dependent and not causally identified. The period ends in 2000.

entries.title: Misallocation and Manufacturing TFP in China and India
entries.method: Monopolistic-competition model with plant-level distortions. Revenue productivity (TFPR) should be equal across plants absent distortions, so dispersion in TFPR is used to measure misallocation within 4-digit industries. The counterfactual reallocates capital and labor until TFPR dispersion matches the U.S. level (the "U.S. efficiency" benchmark), and the aggregate manufacturing TFP gain is computed.
entries.target: Manufacturing plants and firms in China, India and the U.S., within 4-digit manufacturing industries.
entries.period: China 1998-2005 (Annual Surveys of Industrial Production); India 1987-1994 (Annual Survey of Industries, 1987-88 to 1994-95); U.S. 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997 (Census of Manufactures).
entries.quantity: Manufacturing TFP gain in China from moving to U.S. efficiency
entries.quote: we calculate manufacturing TFP gains of 30-50% in China and 40-60% in India.
entries.limitation: Gains are model-based counterfactuals that treat the U.S. as the undistorted benchmark, and TFPR dispersion also reflects measurement error, adjustment costs and markup variation. The periods differ by country (China 1998-2005, India 1987-1994), and the paper does not cover Japan, IT or entry directly.

entries.method: 英国のAnnual Business Inquiry(事業所パネル)にIT支出データを接続した。IT資本ストックは恒久棚卸法で構築し、米国の減耗率とヘドニック価格を使った。生産関数(OLS、事業所固定効果あり・なし)で、ITの産出弾力性が所有形態(米系MNE・非米系MNE・国内)で異なるかを推定した。買収の前後比較、GMMシステム推定量、MNE本国の労働規制との交互作用も使った。
entries.target: 英国(UK)の事業所。米国系多国籍企業、非米国系多国籍企業、英国国内企業を比較。ほぼ全民間部門で、小売・卸売・印刷出版などのIT集約部門を含む。

entries.quantity: US ownership vs UK domestic and non-US MNE productivity dummies (no IT term)
entries.quote: US establishments are 7.1% more productive than UK domestic establishments and non-US multinationals are 3.9% more productive.
entries.limitation: 英国の事業所データによる推定であり、日本のデータではない。米系企業の優位を「組織」と解釈するのは、組織を直接測らない間接的な推論である。買収前後の比較でも選別効果を完全には排除できず、期間は1995-2003年に限られる。また、AER出版版が読めなかったため、数値はNBERワーキングペーパー版のものである。

entries.method: Theoretical model of zombie congestion and restructuring. Zombies are identified as firms paying less interest than a hypothetical minimum (subsidized credit). Panel regressions of non-zombie investment (I/K), employment growth and productivity on the industry zombie share, with industry and year dummies, industry-by-year dummies, and a sales-growth control. Counterfactual simulations hold the zombie index at its 1981-1992 average.

entries.title: Zombie Lending and Depressed Restructuring in Japan
entries.method: Zombies are identified as firms receiving subsidized bank credit. A firm counts as a zombie if its actual interest payments fall below a hypothetical minimum. entries.title: Unconditional Convergence in Manufacturing
entries.method: 産業別労働生産性の成長率を初期対数生産性に回帰する。産業固定効果を入れた無条件収束（国固定効果なし）と、国固定効果を加えた条件付き収束を比べる。標準誤差は国レベルでクラスターする。別に127産業それぞれの個別回帰も推定した。
entries.target: UNIDO INDSTAT4の4桁ISIC製造業（約127産業）、先進国・途上国。10年回帰は40か国、5年回帰は72か国。日本は標本国一覧にあるが個別推定値はない。
entries.period: 1990年以降。10年期間と5年期間の成長率を使い、各国の直近期間をプールしたものがベースライン。個別期間は1990-2000から2002-2007まで。
entries.quantity: ベースライン無条件収束係数（10年、プール）
entries.unit: 年率の成長率/対数初期生産性
entries.quote: The estimates from the baseline (pooled) specifications are -3.0 and -5.6 percent, for the 10- and 5-year regressions respectively.
entries.limitation: 読んだのは公刊版ではなく2011年のWP版で、公刊版では推定値が変わっている可能性が高い（検索結果の要約では基準値2.9%・118か国）。産業と期間の限られたUNIDO調査データで、公式部門に限られ、識別も弱い。

entries.title: A Contribution to the Empirics of Economic Growth
entries.method: Solow模型の定常状態から導いた式を、クロスカントリーでOLS推定した。説明変数はln(I/GDP)とln(n+g+δ)で、g+δ=0.05と仮定した。ln(s)とln(n+g+δ)の係数が逆符号で等しいという制約の検定も行った。次に人的資本(中等教育在学率SCHOOL)を加えた拡張Solow模型を推定した。さらに初期所得ln(Y60)を入れた条件付き収束の回帰で収束速度λを推定した。
entries.target: 1960-85年の国際クロスカントリーデータ。非産油国98か国、中間標本75か国(データ品質Dや人口100万未満を除外)、OECD22か国(人口100万超)。日本は3標本すべてに含まれる(表A-I)。産業別の分析はない。
entries.period: 1960-1985年。投資率と人口増加率は1960-85年平均。被説明変数は1985年の生産年齢人口1人当たりGDPの対数、または1960-85年の対数差。
entries.quantity: 教科書版Solow模型の制約付き回帰で含意される資本分配率α(中間標本)
entries.quote: the α implied by the coefficient in the constrained regression for the intermediate sample is .59 (with a standard error of .02)
entries.limitation: 横断面OLSで内生性(投資率や就学率と技術水準の同時決定)の識別が弱く、技術水準が国間で同一という仮定を置き、データは1960-85年に限られる。日本は単独では推定されず、1985年までで止まり、IT・規制・参入は扱われない。また今回読んだのはNBERワーキングペーパー版で、QJE刊行版の数値と一致するかは未確認。

entries.title: Distance to Frontier, Selection, and Economic Growth
entries.method: This is a theoretical model, not an estimation. Managers both adapt technologies from the world frontier and innovate, and selecting high-skill managers matters more for innovation. Countries near the frontier shift from an investment-based strategy to an innovation-based one. The model also covers non-convergence traps under endogenous policy. Empirical content is limited to descriptive PPP GDP-per-worker comparisons from the Penn World Tables, used as motivating cases in footnotes.
entries.target: Stylized cross-country cases. Japan (MITI and the keiretsu) and South Korea (the chaebol) as investment-based growth. Brazil, Peru, Mexico, Hong Kong and Singapore as convergence or stagnation comparisons.
entries.period: 1950 to 2000 (Penn World Tables). Hong Kong and Singapore from 1960.
entries.quantity: Brazil GDP per worker relative to US, 1950
entries.quote: Brazil and Peru started with GDP per worker levels equal to, respectively, 18% and 22% of the U.S. in 1950.
entries.limitation: This is the 2002 NBER working paper, not the 2006 JEEA text. It contains no econometric estimates, so the numbers are descriptive footnote statistics with no standard errors or identification, and Japan's role is narrative only.

entries.title: When Fast-Growing Economies Slow Down: International Evidence and Implications for China
entries.method: The authors define a slowdown as a year in which the 7-year average per capita growth before the year is at least 3.5%, growth falls by at least 2 percentage points between the preceding and following 7 years, and per capita GDP exceeds $10,000 (2005 PPP). They list the slowdown cases (Table 1), then estimate probit regressions of slowdown likelihood on income, prior growth, demographics, trade openness, spending composition, and policy variables (inflation, real undervaluation). They apply the estimates to China.
entries.target: Cross-country sample of fast-growing economies built from Penn World Table data. The sample includes Japan (slowdowns centered on 1970 and 1992), Hong Kong, Singapore, Norway, Austria, Spain and others. China is the target of the out-of-sample application.
entries.period: Penn World Table 6.3 data, 1957-2007. Slowdown years are identified over this window.
entries.quantity: Mean per capita GDP at which slowdowns occur
entries.quote: the mean income at which slowdowns occur falls from $16,740 to $15,092 when we reduce the minimum-income threshold from $10,000 to $7,500
entries.limitation: Slowdown dates come from a mechanical threshold rule on 7-year averages, and the regressions are probit associations rather than causal identification. The sample ends in 2007 and mixes oil exporters with very different countries, so the Japan and China applications are extrapolation. I read the NBER working-paper version, not the published article.

entries.title: International Technology Diffusion
entries.method: Literature survey of the endogenous-technological-change literature on international technology diffusion. It covers reduced-form R&D-spillover regressions (Coe-Helpman type), the Eaton-Kortum structural general-equilibrium model, and channels such as trade, FDI, communication and geography. It does no original estimation.
entries.target: Review article. The main subjects are OECD countries, the G-7 and G-5 (including Japan and the US), and 22 industrialized countries. Some FDI studies cover the UK and the US-Japan FDI link. Developing countries are discussed qualitatively.
entries.period: Reviewed studies cover roughly 1970 to 1995. Examples are Eaton-Kortum around 1988 and Keller 2001a over 1983-1995. The review itself is dated October 2001 (working paper).
entries.quantity: US lead in per-capita income over Japan
entries.quote: the U.S.' lead in per capita income over Japan has increased from 10% in 1990 to 20% by 1999
entries.limitation: These figures come from the 2001 NBER working-paper version rather than the JEL text, are second-hand results from cross-country reduced-form or structural models with weak causal identification, cover only 1970-1995 data, and are not Japan-specific except the Eaton-Kortum G-5 share.

entries.title: Information technology and the Japanese economy
entries.method: Growth accounting on a production possibility frontier (Jorgenson 1995c, 2002). Output growth is the share-weighted growth of IT and non-IT inputs plus TFP. IT-sector TFP is measured by the dual (price) approach from relative price changes. New Japanese software investment data and adjusted IT price indexes were built for comparability with U.S. NIPA. 2003-2013 growth projections use base, optimistic and pessimistic scenarios. No standard errors or confidence intervals are reported, because these are accounting decompositions rather than regression estimates.
entries.target: Japan and the United States, whole economy (aggregate GDP). Japanese data adjusted to U.S. NIPA definitions, with the IT sector split into computers, software and communications equipment.
entries.quantity: Contribution of IT capital services to GDI growth, Japan
entries.quote: The contribution of IT capital in Japan during this period was 0.54 percent per year, while the corresponding figure for the U.S. was 0.88 percent.
entries.limitation: This is aggregate growth accounting with no standard errors. It rests on assumed competitive markets and constant returns, and on constructed Japanese IT price and software series. It shows no causal link from IT to the slowdown, no firm or industry detail on entry or regulation, and the data end in 2003.

entries.title: An Exploration of Technology Diffusion
entries.method: The authors build a technology-adoption model that matches the one-sector neoclassical growth model at the aggregate level. The model's reduced-form equation for adoption measures (units of capital or output using a technology) has a non-linear trend term that identifies each technology-country adoption lag. They estimate it by country and technology and then decompose the variance of lags with fixed effects. A development-accounting exercise then feeds the estimated country lags into the model's steady-state income equation.
entries.target: 15 technologies in 166 countries, covering transportation, telecommunication, IT, health care, steel production and electricity. Japan, the OECD, the East Asian Tigers and others are compared. Cross-country data come from Comin, Hobijn and Rovito (2006).
entries.period: 1820-2003 (data on technologies invented from 1788 to 1983)
entries.quantity: Speed-up in adoption for newer technologies
entries.unit: years faster per ten-year-later invention date
entries.quote: technologies invented ten years later are on average adopted 4.3 years faster.
entries.limitation: The numbers come from the April 2008 working-paper draft rather than the AER version. The identification relies on a functional-form assumption (a non-linear trend in the adoption measure), and the lags are estimated for only about two thirds of pairs. Poor countries are likely biased towards short lags. The 15-technology sample is mostly transport and communication, and the income accounting assumes this sample represents all technologies. Table 4's country-group lags are given only as printed (they appear to be relative to a benchmark) and are not extracted.

entries.title: The New Economics of Industrial Policy
entries.method: 産業政策の実証文献レビュー。因果識別(自然実験、回帰不連続、差の差)を用いた近年研究と、測定(支出会計、介入件数、テキスト分類)を整理し、東アジア経験を再評価する。本論文自体は新規推定を行わない。
entries.target: サーベイ論文。米国(WW2工場、公的R&D)、韓国(HCI政策)、日本(Technopolis、MITI)、中国、欧州(Criscuolo系の地域政策)など。特定産業ではなく製造業・戦略産業全般。
entries.period: 引用研究の期間は1930年代〜2022年。産業政策支出の測定は2019年、介入件数は2010-2022年。
entries.quantity: 産業政策支出の対GDP比(中国)
entries.quote: DiPippo et al. estimate that in 2019 China spent about 1.5% of its GDP on industrial policy versus 0.3-0.7% of GDP in the other economies.
entries.limitation: 本論文はサーベイで、数値は他論文の推定の再掲であり、日本の停滞・IT・参入・規制に直接かかる推定値はほとんどなく、地域・年代・手法の異なる研究を並べているため日本へ直接外挿できない。

entries.quantity: 制限付きFDI(合弁条件)による提携国内メーカーの車種品質への効果(中国自動車、2007-2014)

entries.title: Industrial Policy and Competition
entries.method: Firm-level panel regressions of log TFP (OLS with firm fixed effects and Olley-Pakes) on industrial policies (subsidies, tax holidays, subsidized loans, tariffs). Competition is the Lerner Index. Policy dispersion across firms in a city-industry is measured as one minus the Herfindahl (CompHerf). Policy is also interacted with initial competition, with age and size targeting, and with firm-specific price deflators. Reallocation terms are examined in Table 7. Source read: NBER PDF of w18048, revised January 2015 AEJ version.
entries.target: China, all medium and large manufacturing enterprises (firm-level census data)
entries.quantity: TFP effect of a perfectly dispersed subsidy allocation (CompHerf subsidies, Table 4 col 1)
entries.quote: a perfectly dispersed set of subsidies, leading to a Herfindahl for subsidies of zero and consequently the complement of that at 1, would increase TFP by 3.9 percentage points.
entries.limitation: The estimates are correlations from Chinese manufacturing in 1998-2007, with limited identification and revenue-based TFP; the authors themselves note that the revenue-based TFP could reflect price or markup changes, so transfer to Japan's stagnation, IT and regulation is weak.

entries.title: Is foreign direct investment a channel of knowledge spillovers? Evidence from Japan's FDI in the United States
entries.method: Firm-level panel using U.S. patent citations as a measure of knowledge spillovers. Citations by Japanese firms' patents to the U.S. patent stock are spillovers to Japan. Citations by U.S.-invented patents to Japanese firms' patents are spillovers from Japan. Poisson and negative binomial fixed-effects count models with year dummies. Controls are log R&D, log sales and log U.S. patents; Tables 4 and 5 add time-varying technological proximity, and Table 5 adds an age measure. FDI is measured as cumulative counts of all U.S. affiliates, acquired affiliates, or R&D/product-development facilities. Supported by interviews with Japanese R&D managers.
entries.target: Japanese manufacturing firms' FDI (U.S. affiliates) and patent citations to and from U.S.-invented patents. Country pair: Japan to the United States. Industry: manufacturing firms, with sales from the Japan Development Bank Corporate Finance Database.
entries.period: The quantitative data end in 1994 (p.14: "my quantitative data, which end in 1994"). The start year of the panel was not found in the pages I read. FDI counts come from the 1997 edition of Kaigai Shinshutsu Kigyou Souran. Interviews were held in fall 2000.
entries.quantity: Spillovers TO Japanese firms: FDI coefficient, all U.S. affiliates, negative binomial fixed effects (1)
entries.unit: semi-elasticity coefficient (log citations per additional affiliate)
entries.locator: Table 2, p.24, NB Fixed Effects(1), Obs=2093
entries.limitation: Fixed-effects count models cannot rule out reverse causation or unobserved time-varying firm changes, results are not stable across FDI measures or lag structures (the total-FDI coefficient is insignificant in Table 2), the data end in 1994, FDI is measured as unweighted counts, and the article was read from the 2000 working-paper version, not the 2006 published one.

entries.title: Is Japan's Innovative Capacity in Decline?
entries.method: Fixed-effects negative binomial regressions of firm patent counts (US grants by application year; citation-adjusted with 4-year citations; Japanese applications) on log R&D and year dummies. Year-dummy path is the productivity trend. Also fixed-effects NB regressions of citations to US patents on US alliances (spillovers), and of citation-adjusted output on knowledge flows. Interviews with R&D managers supplement this.
entries.target: Japan, manufacturing firms (panel of nearly 200 firms, electronics vs other manufacturing)
entries.period: 1980s-1990s; regression year dummies 1982-1997 (US patent data 1980-1999)
entries.quantity: Year dummy 1989, US patent counts (Table 1 col 1), coefficient
entries.quote: Fixed effects negative binomial regression models Obs=2,726
entries.limitation: Patents are an imperfect output measure, the sample over-represents large R&D-intensive firms, the alliance and knowledge-flow results are correlational (the authors say they are not strong causal evidence), and the post-1995 citation-adjusted decline is partly a truncation artifact.

entries.method: 事業所レベルのコブ=ダグラス型生産関数(被説明変数は一人当たり産出の対数)に、IT資本と米国系所有ダミーの交互作用を入れて推定した。OLSに加え、事業所固定効果、GMM(system)、買収前後の比較を使った。さらに欧州の経営慣行調査(人的資源管理)を結合し、米国系のIT生産性の優位が経営慣行で説明されるかを検定した。
entries.target: 英国の事業所パネル(製造業・サービス業。金融を除く民間部門、ABI)。加えて欧州7か国(仏・独・伊・ポーランド・ポルトガル・スウェーデン・英)の経営慣行調査。比較対象は米国系多国籍企業、非米国系多国籍企業、英国内資企業。マクロ背景は米国と欧州の労働生産性。
entries.period: 英国事業所パネルは1995-2003年(表注: The time period is 1995-2003)。欧州パネルは1999-2006年。マクロ比較は1980-1995年と1995-2006年。

entries.title: Americans Do IT Better: US Multinationals and the Productivity Miracle
entries.method: 事業所レベルのコブ=ダグラス型生産関数(被説明変数は一人当たり産出の対数)に、IT資本と米国系所有ダミーの交互作用を入れて推定した。OLSに加え、事業所固定効果、GMM(system)、買収前後の比較を使った。さらに欧州の経営慣行調査(人的資源管理)を結合し、米国系のIT生産性の優位が経営慣行で説明されるかを検定した。

entries.title: Why was Japan left behind in the ICT revolution?
entries.method: Merged METI Basic Survey and IT Survey firm data, about 22,000 firm-year observations. Pooled OLS Cobb-Douglas production function (ln gross value added on lnK, lnL, lnICT) with firm-size and firm-age group interaction terms, plus year and industry dummies. Marginal product of ICT input derived by firm-size and firm-age group. Descriptive survey evidence on barriers: BPO market, ICT experts, liquidity constraints, ICT literacy.
entries.target: Japan, firm-level data on manufacturing and non-manufacturing industries (27 industries), with a six-economy sector-level TFP comparison in the introduction (Japan, Germany, France, UK, Italy, US).
entries.period: Firm data 1995-2007 (pooled). Sector TFP comparison 1980-1995, 1995-2001, 2001-2008.
entries.quantity: ICT-producing sector share of total labor input (hours worked), Japan, 1995-2007
entries.quote: the average labor input share (hours worked) of the ICT-producing sector in Japan’s total labor input in 1995‒2007 was only 4.1%
entries.limitation: The estimates come from the 2015 RIETI working paper (not the journal text) and from pooled OLS on surveyed firms with at least 50 employees and 30 million yen capital, 1995-2007. Identification is weak (no instruments, input endogeneity, no price adjustment by group, very large and skewed marginal products), and there is no cross-country firm-level comparison.

entries.title: Regulation, productivity and growth: OECD evidence
entries.method: Panel regressions of industry-level multifactor productivity (MFP) growth by country, industry and year. The model is a catch-up (technology gap) specification with country, industry and time dummies. Regressors are the gap to the industry's technology leader, leader MFP growth and human capital. Regulation enters as new OECD quantitative indicators: economy-wide product market regulation, industry-level barriers to entry, entry liberalisation and privatisation. These are interacted with the technology gap. The paper also shows bivariate cross-country correlations and policy simulations based on the regressions.
entries.target: 18 OECD countries, including Japan: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, France, West Germany, Greece, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, UK, US. The industry panel has 17 manufacturing and 6 business services industries.
entries.period: Industry panel regressions cover 1984-1998. The aggregate growth comparison covers the 1980s and 1990s (1980-1990 vs 1990-2000).
entries.quantity: Effect of privatisation on MFP growth (coefficient, overall privatisation)
entries.quote: Overall privatisation i t 0.23 ** 0.24 ** 0.24 **
entries.limitation: The Japan-specific evidence is limited to scatter-plot positions and descriptive statements. The regression coefficients are pooled across 18 countries, many are only 10%-significant, regulation data for several countries had to be proxied, and the sample ends in 1998, so the Japan results do not cover the post-bubble stagnation or the ICT boom.

entries.title: The Industry Origins of the US-Japan Productivity Gap
entries.method: Industry-level growth accounting and level comparison of total factor productivity (TFP) between the US and Japan. It uses a US-Japan bilateral input-output table and industry-level purchasing power parities (PPPs) for capital, labor, energy, materials and output. The PPPs rest on 164 commodities, 33 assets (including land and inventories) and 1596 labor categories. The gap is allocated to industries through Domar-weighted industry TFP levels.
entries.target: US and Japan, whole economy plus 42 common industries. The text refers to 40 industries in places. It singles out IT-producing industries (computers, communications equipment, electronic components), IT-using industries, Wholesale and Retail Trade, and Other Services.
entries.quantity: Japan TFP relative to US, 1960 (Japan/US)
entries.quote: Total Factor Productivity 52.4 72.5 75.4 86.1 82.6 81.7 79.5
entries.limitation: I read the working-paper version rather than the journal text, and the results are accounting decompositions rather than causal estimates. They depend on industry-level PPP measurement, and the attribution to IT is descriptive. The data end in 2004, and the paper reports no standard errors or confidence intervals.

entries.title: Zombie Lending and Depressed Restructuring in Japan
entries.method: A firm is labelled a zombie when its actual interest payments fall below a hypothetical minimum. In Table 3 the crisp definition is used (d1=d2=0). Industry zombie share is the share of industry assets held by zombie firms. Firm-level OLS regressions of investment rate, employment growth and a productivity proxy on a non-zombie dummy, the industry zombie share and their interaction (phi). Specifications add year and industry dummies, then industry-year dummies, then firm sales growth. White standard errors are reported. Counterfactuals extrapolate the coefficients for five non-manufacturing industries.
entries.target: Japan: publicly traded firms in manufacturing, construction, real estate, wholesale/retail and services (Tokyo Stock Exchange first and second sections)
entries.period: 1981-2002 (firm-level regressions use 1993-2002 for the non-zombie counterfactuals; the sample has 1,844 to 2,506 firms per year)
entries.quantity: Aggregate zombie percentage (all firms, equal weight), 1994 onward
entries.value_raw: above 25 percent for every year after 1994
entries.quote: the percentage of zombies hovered between 5 and 15 percent up until 1993 and then rose sharply over the mid 1990s so that the zombie percentage was above 25 percent for every year after 1994
entries.limitation: The estimates are reduced-form correlations on listed firms only (no private firms or entrants), and the industry zombie share could proxy for unobserved industry-year conditions. Significance is weaker with industry-year dummies and sales controls: the employment phi is significant only at the 6 percent level, then at the 20 percent level with sales growth. The counterfactuals ignore general equilibrium effects. The US Compustat check found no significant phi, and the study covers only Japan, 1981-2002.

entries.title: The 1990s in Japan: A Lost Decade
entries.method: Growth accounting plus a calibrated neoclassical growth model (Hansen-style, with workweek length h exogenous). entries.title: WHY DID JAPAN'S TFP GROWTH SLOW DOWN IN THE LOST DECADE? AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS BASED ON FIRM-LEVEL DATA OF MANUFACTURING FIRMS
entries.method: TFP growth is decomposed with the Baily-Hulten-Campbell / Foster-Haltiwanger-Krizan method into within, between, covariance, entry and exit effects (with switch-in and switch-out). Gross-output TFP is computed per firm. The TFP gap between the 75th and 25th percentile firms is tracked by industry and year. Firm-level OLS regressions on TFP growth use R&D intensity, internationalization, ownership, size and the liability-asset ratio, plus beta-convergence. Cross-country comparison covers the US, Korea, Finland, France, Italy and the Netherlands. IT adoption is not analyzed.
entries.target: Japan, manufacturing sector (30 industries), firm-level data from the METI Basic Survey on Business Activities by Enterprises (Kigyo Katsudo Kihon Chosa)
entries.period: 1994-2001 (regressions on annual TFP growth 1995-2001)
entries.quantity: Manufacturing TFP growth total, 1994-2001 (Japan, firm-level decomposition)
entries.limitation: The analysis covers manufacturing only for 1994-2001 using a METI survey with size cut-offs (so exit includes shrinking, merging or switching firms), and the regressions are correlational with weak identification of causality; IT effects are explicitly not analyzed, and the text read is the 2005 RIETI working-paper version rather than the published JER article.

entries.title: Americans Do IT Better: US Multinationals and the Productivity Miracle
entries.method: Establishment-level production function regressions with IT capital (perpetual inventory) interacted with ownership dummies (US multinational, non-US multinational, domestic). Includes establishment fixed effects, Olley-Pakes and GMM checks, and a pre/post-takeover comparison. A dynamic model of organization and IT with country-specific adjustment costs is added.
entries.target: UK establishments (about 8% US-owned multinationals, 31% non-US multinationals, 61% domestic) across production and services, with comparison to US and European macro productivity. Japan is not analysed; it appears only in a list in the appendix.
entries.period: 1995 to 2003 (UK Annual Business Inquiry matched to IT expenditure surveys; many more observations after 1999)
entries.quantity: Raw labor productivity premium of multinational establishments over the 3-digit industry average (2001)
entries.quote: Labor productivity, as measured by output per employee, is 24% higher for US multinational establishments and 15% higher for non-US multinational establishments.
entries.limitation: The data cover only UK establishments in 1995-2003, they over-represent large establishments, and identification rests on selection-on-observables and takeover timing (no instrument for takeovers). The authors say they cannot rule out other explanations, Japan is not studied, and I read the 2007 working paper rather than the published 2012 AER text.
